etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English elefant, elefaunt, from Old French elefant, elefan, olifant, re-latinized in Middle French as elephant, from Latin elephantus, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās) (gen. ἐλέφαντος (eléphantos)). Believed to be derived from an Afroasiatic form such as Proto-Berber *eḷu (“elephant”) (compare Tamahaq êlu, Tamasheq alu) or Egyptian ꜣbw (“elephant; ivory”). More at ivory. Replaced Middle English olifant (from the aforementioned Old French form, from Vulgar Latin *olifantus), which replaced Old English elpend (“elephant”).

definitions.definition: A mammal of the order Proboscidea, having a trunk, and two large ivory tusks jutting from the upper jaw.

quote.citation: 1613, Thomas Heywood, The Brazen Age, […], London:  […]  Nicholas Okes, […], →OCLC, Act II, signature [C4], verso:
quote.text: She [Diana] hath ſent (to plague vs) a huge ſauadge Boare, / Of an vn-meaſured height and magnitude. /  […]  / His briſtles poynted like a range of pikes / Ranck't on his backe: his foame ſnovves vvhere he feeds / His tuskes are like the Indian Oliphants.

definitions.definition: (in particular) Any member of the subfamily Elephantinae not also of the genera Mammuthus and Primelephas.
(British, childish) used when counting to add length, so that each count takes about one second

definitions.definition: (xiangqi) A xiangqi piece that is moved two points diagonally, may not jump over intervening pieces and may not cross the river.
